questions.knowledge_point: Identifying the Formula For Negating a Quantified Statement
questions.worked_solution:
To negate the universal statement $∀m\in T,\,S(m),$ we flip the quantifier to existential and negate the predicate:

$$
¬(∀m\in T,\,S(m))≡∃m\in T,\,¬S(m)
$$

questions.problem:
Negate the following statement:

$\,$ All prime numbers are not divisible by $5.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $P$ be the set of prime numbers. The given statement can be re-phrased as follows:

$\,$ For all $x\in P,$ $x$ is not divisible by $5.$

Introducing the universal quantifier, we get the following:

$\,$ $∀x\in P,\,x\text{ is not divisible by }5.$

Negating this, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(∀x\in P,\,x\text{ is not divisible by }5.) & ≡∃x\in P,\,¬(x\text{ is not divisible by }5.) \\  & ≡∃x\in P,\,x\text{ is divisible by }5.\end{aligned}
$$

which reads 

$\,$ There exists $x\in P$ such that $x$ is divisible by $5.$

or simply

$\,$ Some prime numbers are divisible by $5.$

choices.value: Some prime numbers are not divisible by $5.$
All prime numbers are divisible by $5.$
Some prime numbers are divisible by $5.$
All prime numbers are not divisible by $5.$

answer_fields.correct_value: Some prime numbers are divisible by $5.$

questions.problem:
Negate the following statement:

$\,$ For all $r\in Q,$ $r\ne \frac{1}{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
If we denote

$$
P(r):r=\frac{1}{2},
$$

our statement can be written as

$$
∀r\in Q,\,¬P(r).
$$

Negating this, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(∀r\in Q,\,¬P(r)) & ≡∃r\in Q,\,¬¬P(r) \\  & ≡∃r\in Q,\,P(r).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $∃r\in Q,\,P(r)$ reads as follows:

$\,$ **There exists** $r\in Q$ such that $r=\frac{1}{2}.$

questions.problem:
Negate the following statement:

$\,$ All rational numbers are positive.
questions.worked_solution:
The given statement can be re-phrased as follows:

$\,$ For all $x\in Q,$ $x$ is positive.

Introducing the universal quantifier, we get the following:

$\,$ $∀x\in Q,\,x\text{ is positive}.$

Negating this, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(∀x\in Q,\,x\text{ is positive}) & ≡∃x\in Q,\,¬(x\text{ is positive}) \\  & ≡∃x\in Q,\,x\text{ is not positive}\end{aligned}
$$

which reads 

$\,$ There exists $x\in Q$ such that $x$ is not positive.

or simply

$\,$ At least one rational number is not positive.

questions.problem:
Negate the following statement: 

$\,$ At least one prime number is not divisible by $5.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $P$ be the set of all prime numbers. The given statement can be re-phrased as follows:

$\,$ There exists $p\in P$ such that $5∤p.$

Introducing the existential quantifier, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(∃p\in P,\,5∤p) & ≡∀p\in P,\,¬(5∤p) \\  & ≡∀p\in P,\,5∣p\end{aligned}
$$

which reads 

$\,$ For all $p\in P,$ $5∣p.$

canonical_examples.problem:
What is the negation of the following statement?

$$
\forall y \in \overline{S}, \, \neg P(y)
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To negate the universal statement $\forall y \in \overline{S}, \, \neg P(y),$ we flip the quantifier to existential and negate the predicate: 

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(∀y\in \overset{―}{S},\,¬P(y)) & ≡∃y\in \overset{―}{S},\,¬¬P(y) \\  & ≡∃y\in \overset{―}{S},\,P(y)\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Negate the following statement:

$\qquad$ For all $n \in \mathbb{N},$ $n$ is a composite number.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
If we denote

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14108273/assets/b8d152c4a9f69b2a6ea0657d9e66ca4adbc11bc480d25a28ea07eac28a646ac3.png)

our statement can be written as

$$
\forall n \in \mathbb{N}, \, P(n).
$$

Negating this, we obtain

$$
\neg \left( \forall n \in \mathbb{N}, \, P(n)  \right) \equiv \exists n \in \mathbb{N}, \, \neg P(n).
$$

Finally, $\exists n \in \mathbb{N}, \, \neg P(n)$ reads as follows:

$\qquad$ **There exists** $n \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $n$ is **not** a composite number.

canonical_examples.problem:
Negate the following statement: 

$\qquad$ Some quadrilaterals are squares.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let $Q$ be the set of all quadrilaterals and $S$ the set of all squares. The given statement can be re-phrased as follows:

$\qquad$ There exists $q \in Q$ such that $q \in S$

Introducing the existential quantifier, we get the following:

$\qquad$ $\exists q \in Q, \, q \in S.$

Negating this, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(∃q\in Q,\,q\in S) & ≡∀q\in Q,\,¬(q\in S) \\  & ≡∀q\in Q,\,q\notin S\end{aligned}
$$

which reads 

$\qquad$ For all $q \in Q,$ $q \not\in S.$

or simply

$\qquad$ All quadrilaterals are not squares.
